analysis.one_liner: Bars the EPA from limiting carbon pollution from power plants and factories for two years.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee on January 31, 2011, never received a committee vote or floor action, and died when the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have stopped the EPA for two years from using the Clean Air Act to regulate carbon dioxide and methane from stationary sources like power plants, refineries, and factories. It would also have wiped out, retroactively, any earlier EPA step that treated those gases as pollutants businesses must account for. Rules for cars and trucks, and paper reporting requirements, would have kept going. The bill never got past the committee it was sent to.
analysis.who_benefits: Large stationary emitters of greenhouse gases: coal-fired electric utilities, oil refiners, cement plants, and other industrial facilities. They would have gotten a two-year reprieve from Clean Air Act permitting requirements and new-source performance standards for carbon dioxide and methane, avoiding the cost of installing controls or changing fuel plans during that window.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Coal and utility power plant operators

how_it_helps.text: For two years after enactment, the EPA could not take any action under the Clean Air Act on stationary-source permitting or on new-source performance standards as they relate to carbon dioxide or methane [S2][S3].

It went further than a simple delay: any EPA action taken before the end of the two years — including actions already taken before the bill passed — could not be considered to make carbon dioxide or methane a regulated pollutant for any source other than cars and trucks [S3].
Vehicle emissions standards, greenhouse-gas reporting requirements, and technical help a state asks for were exempted from the freeze, so the restrictions fell only on stationary sources [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, the public would have borne two more years of uncontrolled carbon and methane emissions from power plants and heavy industry, and the attendant air-quality and climate costs. Businesses planning around upcoming federal rules would also have faced two more years of uncertainty about whether those rules would arrive.
analysis.who_pays_short: People breathing plant and factory emissions

drawbacks.text: It would have delayed federal limits on carbon and methane from the largest stationary emitters — power plants and refineries — for two years, while leaving the greenhouse gases those sources emit in the air [S2][S3].
The retroactive clause would have erased the legal effect of EPA steps already taken to regulate those gases from stationary sources, not just future rules [S3].

An honest supporter would acknowledge the trade: the bill traded avoided compliance costs for utilities against the public's interest in earlier limits on greenhouse-gas emissions from those same facilities.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits flowed to a specific set of large emitters who would avoid permitting and control costs for two years. The costs — two more years of unrestricted emissions from those facilities, and legal uncertainty created by retroactively nullifying prior EPA steps — fell on the public. The bill offered no offsetting public benefit: even greenhouse-gas reporting, the paper requirement, was preserved only as an exception, not expanded.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died when the 112th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator John D. Rockefeller IV of West Virginia introduced the bill on January 31, 2011, joined by six Democratic cosponsors, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works [S5][S3][S4].
The committee took no further action — no markup, no vote, no floor consideration — for the remainder of the 112th Congress [S5].
The bill expired when the Congress ended on January 3, 2013, without ever coming to a vote in either chamber [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The EPA's authority to regulate carbon dioxide and methane from stationary sources was left intact, so the public kept the existing air-quality rules the bill would have frozen or rolled back. Coal-fired utilities and other large emitters gained nothing from the delay they sought, though they also avoided no new rules during the two-year window the bill would have opened.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all six cosponsors were Democrats, most from coal- and energy-producing states, and no Republican cosponsors were listed; no vote was ever taken, so the usual party breakdown never showed itself.

industries.note: The bill would have given them a two-year exemption from Clean Air Act permitting and performance standards for carbon dioxide and methane, the gases their plants emit most, at the cost of delaying limits the public would otherwise face [S2][S3].

Delayed stationary-source rules protect demand for coal by putting off the compliance costs that push utilities toward cleaner fuels; the bill was led and cosponsored by senators from coal states [S3][S4].

industries.industry: Oil refiners, cement, and other large industrial emitters
industries.note: As major stationary sources, they would have avoided the same permitting and new-source standards for two years [S2][S3].
